paper.title: ViBMR: A Large-Scale Multi-Sequence Brain MRI Dataset and Comprehensive Evaluation for Vietnamese Radiology Report Generation
paper.summary: Automated radiology report generation for multi-sequence brain MRI holds strong promise for alleviating radiologists' workload, yet it remains a demanding problem: brain MRI studies are inherently volumetric, each pulse sequence carries complementary diagnostic information, and annotated data are critically scarce for low-resource clinical languages. Existing brain MRI-report resources are still dominated by English reports, translated clinical text, or datasets adapted from task-specific imaging benchmarks, leaving routine low-resource clinical reporting and heterogeneous multi-sequence MRI protocols insufficiently represented. To bridge this gap, we introduce ViBMR, to the best of our knowledge, the first large-scale multi-sequence brain MRI dataset paired with routine Vietnamese clinical reports, comprising 3,649 patients and 11,875 MRI series across T1, T2, FLAIR, and contrast-enhanced T1 sequences. Building on ViBMR, we establish a comprehensive evaluation setup for brain MRI report generation, covering representative medical vision-language models, multi-sequence inputs, and feature aggregation strategies. The results provide key insights into dataset characteristics and model behavior, while demonstrating the necessity of native low-resource clinical datasets for reliable Vietnamese-origin brain MRI report generation. Our dataset and baseline models will be released for non-commercial research.
paper.comment: Accepted at IEEE/CVF Winter Conference on Applications of Computer Vision (WACV 2027)

analysis.executive_summary: This paper addresses the critical gap in medical AI for non-English, low-resource languages by introducing ViBMR, the first large-scale dataset pairing multi-sequence brain MRI with native Vietnamese clinical reports. It provides a comprehensive evaluation framework for medical vision-language models in this specific domain, demonstrating that translated or English-dominant data is insufficient for reliable local clinical reporting.

paper.title: Stochastic Nonlinearities Improve Uncertainty Estimation
paper.summary: Reliable uncertainty estimation is important across visual recognition tasks, providing information about the confidence and reliability of model predictions. Many uncertainty estimation methods obtain predictive diversity through mechanisms that can suppress intermediate features, perturb the input, or require substantial additional computation. Stochastic activation functions, where network units randomly select between multiple nonlinearities during a forward pass, have previously been used to improve optimization behavior, mitigate limitations of fixed ReLU activations, and increase output diversity. In this work, we reframe stochastic activation switching as a lightweight mechanism for uncertainty estimation. The proposed method samples between nonlinear activation functions, inducing predictive diversity while keeping intermediate feature pathways active. This enables uncertainty estimation from a single trained model without the training cost of ensembles, task-specific uncertainty heads, or architectural redesign. We evaluate the proposed approach across classification, semantic segmentation, and out-of-distribution detection using convolutional and transformer-based architectures on diverse datasets. Across these settings, stochastic activation switching improves uncertainty quality while preserving competitive primary-task performance, showing that stochastic nonlinearities provide an effective and information-preserving source of predictive variation for visual recognition.

analysis.executive_summary: This paper introduces a lightweight mechanism for uncertainty estimation by reframing stochastic activation switching as a source of predictive diversity. It enables robust confidence assessment from a single trained model without the need for ensembles or additional uncertainty heads, maintaining competitive primary-task performance across classification, segmentation, and OOD detection.

paper.title: Compositionality with Primitives: A Unified View from Euclidean to Hyperbolic Vision-Language Models
paper.summary: Compositional zero-shot learning (CZSL) aims to recognize novel combinations of previously observed objects and attributes. Prior work showed that large-scale vision-language models encode decomposable semantic structures that can be recomposed to enable generalization. The Geodesically Decomposable Embeddings (GDE) framework formalizes this by identifying directions in the tangent space at the Frechet mean of the embedding distribution, which encode primitive visual concepts. Unseen attribute-object compositions can be synthesized through vector addition of these primitives. We revisit the assumption that compositional generalization requires explicit attribute-object pair re-composition. By means of new compositional scoring functions and extensive evaluations, we show that directly using the decomposed primitives suffices for recognizing unseen compositions. In that, we gain insights on how the geometry of the embedding manifold (Euclidean, spherical, or hyperbolic) and dataset structure affect compositional reasoning. Across models (CLIP, DINOv2, MERU, HyCoCLIP), we show that compositional structure consistently emerges as primitive representations, enabling inference on CZSL benchmarks (MIT-States, VAW-CZSL, UT-Zappos50K, Clothing16K) and group robustness on Waterbirds and CelebA. Code: https://github.com/nis-research/Compositionality-with-Primitives.
paper.comment: Accepted at WACV 2027 Main Conference, 17 pages, 6 figures, 8 tables

analysis.problem_statement: The paper addresses the challenge of compositional zero-shot learning (CZSL) by demonstrating that explicit re-composition of attribute-object pairs is unnecessary for recognizing novel combinations, as decomposed primitive representations alone suffice.

analysis.executive_summary: This work challenges the standard assumption in CZSL that novel concepts must be synthesized via vector addition of attribute and object primitives. By introducing new scoring functions, it shows that direct use of these primitives enables robust recognition of unseen compositions across various embedding geometries (Euclidean, spherical, hyperbolic). This provides a unified theoretical and practical framework for leveraging the inherent decomposable structure of large-scale vision-language models.

key_metrics.primary_metric: Recognition accuracy on unseen compositions in CZSL benchmarks

paper.title: CountVideoBench: A Benchmark to Evaluate Prediction Biases on the Object Counting task by Video-Language Models
paper.summary: Object counting in videos remains a poorly characterized capability of multimodal large language models. Counting questions are included in many existing VideoQA benchmarks, but the ground-truth count distributions in these benchmarks are heavily skewed toward small values. Across the nine benchmarks we survey, the median ground-truth count is at most five, and the three most frequent values together account for between 45% and 93% of the videos. The resulting mean accuracy is then dominated by the most frequent counts; a value-dependent bias at a rare count contributes negligibly to the average and remains invisible. We introduce CountVideoBench, a benchmark of 2,600 synthetic videos covering 26 cardinalities in the interval [5, 50] (100 videos each), grouped into six clusters of consecutive counts that span the range while enabling near-neighbor comparisons. Each video contains a single class of static objects under a controlled camera motion, removing object motion and reducing recognition as confounds. We evaluate sixteen video-language models from nine architecture families in a zero-shot setting. No model exceeds 27.6% Exact Match. The dependence of accuracy on cardinality varies across models, ranging from monotonic decline to a non-monotonic peak-and-collapse pattern, which rules out increasing difficulty with cardinality as the dominant explanation of counting failure. Every model further concentrates its predictions on its own set of preferred integers, with accuracy peaks coinciding with these values and collapsing at adjacent counts. These findings highlight the need for balanced, diagnostic counting benchmarks to reliably assess this fundamental visual capability.
paper.comment: Accepted at BMVC 2026. Project page: https://countvideobench.github.io

analysis.problem_statement: Existing video-language model benchmarks for object counting suffer from severe class imbalance in ground-truth counts, masking value-dependent prediction biases and rendering mean accuracy an unreliable metric for assessing counting capabilities.
analysis.bottleneck_addressed: Evaluation bias and lack of diagnostic granularity in multimodal benchmarking, specifically regarding numerical reasoning and object counting in video.
analysis.executive_summary: This paper exposes a critical flaw in current VideoQA benchmarks where skewed count distributions hide model-specific biases, such as concentration on preferred integers. By introducing a balanced synthetic benchmark, it reveals that no current video-language model exceeds 27.6% Exact Match, demonstrating that counting failures are driven by model-specific biases rather than just increasing difficulty with cardinality.

paper.title: Unlocking Spatial Grounding in Flow-Matching Models via SNR Tuning
paper.summary: Despite the success of foundation models in image synthesis, achieving fine-grained spatial control remains a significant challenge, typically requiring auxiliary structural adapters or complex inference-time steering. While modern vision-language (VLM) text encoders possess the latent capacity to represent spatial coordinates, generative models often fail to leverage this information. We demonstrate that the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) distribution is a critical determinant of spatial grounding in flow-matching models. Using a novel synthetic benchmark of geometric primitives, we isolate structural mechanics from textural complexity inherent in natural imagery and introduce a rigorous color-aware layout metric to quantify spatial fidelity. We show that training on a centered SNR distribution results in poor layout adherence (25.9%). Instead, we identify high-noise regimes as a "critical learning phase" for spatial grounding. Shifting the training focus toward these stages increases layout adherence to 80.8%, effectively reaching the 83.6% reconstruction ceiling of the underlying variational autoencoder. We find that the necessity for this shift scales with resolution and aspect ratio variance, and that the conservative noise schedules employed by models like FLUX.1 are insufficient for precise layout adherence. Finally, we show that these findings translate to real-world imagery via the COCO dataset (1.0 vs. 57.3 Average Precision), where state-of-the-art layout adherence is unlocked through distribution tuning alone, without architectural modifications.
paper.comment: Accepted at BMVC 2026 (Oral)

analysis.problem_statement: Flow-matching generative models fail to effectively leverage spatial coordinate information from vision-language encoders, resulting in poor fine-grained spatial control and layout adherence.
analysis.bottleneck_addressed: Lack of fine-grained spatial grounding and layout control in text-to-image generation without auxiliary structural adapters.
analysis.executive_summary: This paper identifies the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) distribution as the critical determinant for spatial grounding in flow-matching models. By shifting the training focus toward high-noise regimes, it achieves state-of-the-art layout adherence without architectural modifications, offering a simple yet effective solution to a persistent challenge in generative AI.

key_metrics.baseline: Centered SNR distribution (25.9% layout adherence, 1.0 AP on COCO)
key_metrics.improvement_percentage: 212% improvement in synthetic layout adherence (25.9% to 80.8%)

technical_breakdown.code_complexity: No architectural modifications required; only distribution tuning of the noise schedule, implying minimal computational overhead compared to adding auxiliary adapters.

paper.title: Think-Capture: Active 3D Geometry Acquisition for Spatial Reasoning in Vision-Language Models
paper.summary: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) excel at 2D recognition but often fail to maintain consistent 3D relations across sparse viewpoints, leading to spatial hallucinations under occlusion and perspective changes. Existing methods commonly fuse all frames with dense geometry, incurring substantial computation and context overhead while encouraging blind reliance on imperfect estimators. We present Think-Capture, a query-conditioned framework that first identifies task-critical objects and then acquires their geometry on demand. A 3D toolkit lifts zero-shot masks into a common coordinate frame, and a Symbolic 3D State Abstraction compresses object and camera states into structured text. Hierarchical Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) trains the VLM on cases in which geometry either helps or misleads, teaching it when to use tool evidence and when to fall back on visual cues. Think-Capture-4B reaches 54.4% on MindCube-Tiny (+21.5 points over its backbone), 39.1% on the MMSI-Bench positional subset (+7.9), and 42.8% on ViewSpatial (+5.2). It also remains robust under coordinate and mask perturbations. The full stack fits one 24 GB GPU and serves as an asynchronous high-level reasoner on an Agibot G1. Our code is available at https://github.com/819346675/Think-Capture.
paper.comment: Accepted at WACV 2027

analysis.problem_statement: Vision-Language Models suffer from spatial hallucinations and inconsistent 3D relation reasoning due to the high computational overhead and reliance on imperfect dense geometry estimators when processing sparse viewpoints.
analysis.bottleneck_addressed: Inefficient context management and computational overhead in 3D spatial reasoning, specifically the trade-off between dense geometry fusion and sparse visual cues.
analysis.executive_summary: This paper addresses the critical gap in VLMs' ability to maintain consistent 3D spatial relations by introducing a query-conditioned framework that acquires geometry only for task-critical objects. By using Symbolic 3D State Abstraction and hierarchical reinforcement learning, it enables models to distinguish between helpful and misleading geometric evidence, significantly improving spatial reasoning accuracy while maintaining low computational costs suitable for edge deployment.

key_metrics.baseline: Backbone model (implied as Think-Capture-4B backbone)

technical_breakdown.method: A query-conditioned framework that identifies task-critical objects, lifts zero-shot masks into a common coordinate frame using a 3D toolkit, and compresses states into structured text via Symbolic 3D State Abstraction.
technical_breakdown.architecture: Consists of a 3D toolkit for mask lifting, a Symbolic 3D State Abstraction module for text compression, and a VLM trained with Hierarchical Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO).
technical_breakdown.implementation_details: Uses Hierarchical GRPO to train the VLM on cases where geometry helps or misleads, teaching the model to selectively use tool evidence or fall back on visual cues. The system is designed to fit within a single 24 GB GPU.
technical_breakdown.code_complexity: Low computational overhead compared to dense geometry fusion methods; fits on a single 24 GB GPU and operates as an asynchronous high-level reasoner on Agibot G1.

paper.title: Reference Manual of MEDiml
paper.summary: Radiomics is the high-throughput extraction of quantitative features (e.g., tumor shape, intensity distributions, and texture) from medical images to characterize tissues and uncover disease patterns invisible to the human eye. These features can serve as candidate imaging biomarkers for cancer diagnosis, prognosis, and classification. However, extracting thousands of features makes it difficult to identify the most informative ones for a given clinical task, while implementing an end-to-end workflow can require programming expertise that limits accessibility for clinical researchers. Hence, we propose MEDiml, an open-source, standards-compliant radiomics platform connecting feature extraction, predictive modeling, and interpretation through complementary graphical and programmatic interfaces. MEDiml combines a Python package (MEDiml-pkg) with a graphical desktop application (MEDiml-app) that enables researchers to conduct experiments without writing code. Both interfaces use the same computational implementation, and code generation exports graphically configured workflows as executable Python code, facilitating reproducibility and collaboration between clinical researchers and computational scientists. A typical MEDiml workflow includes image preprocessing, radiomic feature extraction, feature set reduction, model training and evaluation, and interpretation using feature importance. Feature sets can be grouped into levels of radiomic complexity (morphological, intensity-based, textural, and filter-based) to evaluate whether more complex features provide additional predictive value. This reference manual documents the radiomics concepts, workflow, software components, architecture, and installation, compares MEDiml with existing tools, and demonstrates its complexity-driven workflow on five oncological imaging cohorts comprising 2,104 patients. Resources: www.mediml.app.

analysis.bottleneck_addressed: Accessibility and reproducibility in clinical AI workflows, specifically bridging the gap between non-programmer clinical researchers and computational scientists.
analysis.executive_summary: MEDiml provides a unified, open-source platform that combines a graphical user interface with a Python package to streamline the end-to-end radiomics pipeline. By enabling code generation from GUI configurations, it ensures reproducibility while lowering the technical threshold for clinical researchers. The platform introduces a complexity-driven workflow that evaluates the predictive value of different levels of radiomic features across multiple oncological cohorts.

paper.title: Extending FAIR Principles with Observability for Trustworthy Federated Learning
paper.summary: Federated learning (FL) keeps data at its source, but locality alone does not make a federation trustworthy. Without sufficient observability, an aggregator cannot determine whether the client service was healthy, the local data pipeline was trustworthy, or contractual constraints were properly monitored during training. We take the position that trustworthy FL needs an evidence plane in addition to its model-update process. Each participant continuously summarizes local infrastructure, data into minimal, signed trust evidence associated with each FL round, while raw data, logs remain local. A local TinyLLM may assist in interpreting observability signals, deriving contextual evidence, and providing natural-language explanations to operators. We instantiate this vision through FAIR-O, an observability extension of FAIR principle. Rather than benchmarking FL accuracy, a three-level trust model has been proposed and a two-participant Python prototype demonstrates evidence generation and trust assessment. We further discuss future integration of FAIR-O Trust Evidence into participant selection, evidence weighting, and federated aggregation.
paper.comment: The paper has been accepted by TrustFL-SIS 2026 - Trustworthy Federated Learning for Smart Industrial Systems Workshop, co-located with IEEE ICDM 2026,

analysis.problem_statement: Federated learning systems lack sufficient observability to verify the health of client infrastructure, the integrity of local data pipelines, and the enforcement of contractual constraints, thereby undermining trust in the federation.
analysis.bottleneck_addressed: Trust and verifiability in decentralized data processing
analysis.executive_summary: This paper addresses the critical gap in Federated Learning (FL) where data locality does not equate to system trustworthiness. It proposes an 'evidence plane' that generates signed, minimal trust evidence from local observability signals without exposing raw data, enabling aggregators to assess participant reliability. This is significant for industrial FL deployments where regulatory compliance and data integrity are paramount.

key_metrics.primary_metric: Qualitative demonstration of trust assessment via a three-level trust model
key_metrics.baseline: Standard FL without observability extensions

technical_breakdown.method: The system extends FAIR principles to create FAIR-O, where participants continuously summarize local infrastructure and data pipeline status into signed trust evidence associated with each FL round. A local TinyLLM assists in interpreting observability signals and generating natural-language explanations.
technical_breakdown.architecture: Consists of a local observability layer, a TinyLLM for signal interpretation, an evidence generation module producing signed artifacts, and a trust assessment component using a three-level model.
technical_breakdown.implementation_details: A two-participant Python prototype demonstrates the generation of trust evidence and its assessment. The approach relies on minimal signed evidence rather than raw logs or data transmission.
technical_breakdown.code_complexity: Low computational overhead implied by the use of 'minimal' evidence and a 'TinyLLM', though specific complexity metrics are not provided.

paper.title: Velocity Ambiguity Profiles: Time-Resolved Bayes-Risk Diagnostics for Flow Matching
paper.summary: Flow matching trains a continuum of velocity regression problems but usually reports a loss averaged over interpolation time, obscuring which regions are limited by intrinsic ambiguity and which remain data-limited. We introduce the Velocity Ambiguity Profile (VAP), $\mathcal{A}_v(t)$, the time-local Bayes-risk floor of velocity prediction, and decompose time-resolved loss as $L_N(t)=\mathcal{A}_v(t)+R(t;N)$, where only the excess term $R(t;N)$ is reducible by more data or a different estimator. For $N$ training samples and a $K$-component mixture in the structured example, we prove two statistical benchmarks. In an intrinsic local-regression benchmark, $\mathcal{A}_v(t)$ enters the time-dependent noise factor of the standard nonparametric rate. In separated isotropic Gaussian mixtures, the Bayes velocity becomes locally affine, and a label-oracle residual-regression benchmark has parametric excess-risk scale $K\mathcal{A}_v(t)/N$, matched within the same separated residual Gaussian-location subproblem. Controlled Gaussian-mixture experiments validate this diagnostic through a dense transition sweep, calibrated oracle-to-blind and empirical-proxy audits, and a local controlled time-sampler stress test in which a frozen reducible-error proxy reduces reducible loss while cross-cell sensitivity delimits aggressive sampling. On CIFAR-100 DINOv2 feature flow, guided time sampling reduces uniformly evaluated velocity loss by $6.78\%$ and global feature Fréchet distance (FD) by $23.6\%$, while class-conditional kernel inception distance (KID) shows no improvement. VAP turns an averaged flow-matching objective into a time-resolved diagnostic for locating ambiguity-limited and data-limited regions.
paper.comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026

analysis.problem_statement: Standard flow matching training obscures which regions of the interpolation time are limited by intrinsic data ambiguity versus reducible estimation error, preventing targeted optimization of the training process.
analysis.bottleneck_addressed: Inefficient data utilization and lack of diagnostic granularity in generative model training, specifically regarding the trade-off between intrinsic noise and sample complexity.
analysis.executive_summary: This paper introduces the Velocity Ambiguity Profile (VAP) to decompose flow matching loss into an irreducible Bayes-risk floor and a reducible excess term, enabling precise identification of data-limited regions. By guiding time sampling based on this diagnostic, the method significantly improves feature space metrics like Fréchet Distance without relying on increased data volume, offering a principled approach to optimizing generative training efficiency.

key_metrics.primary_metric: Global feature Fréchet Distance (FD) reduction on CIFAR-100 DINOv2 feature flow
key_metrics.baseline: Uniformly evaluated velocity loss / standard flow matching training

technical_breakdown.method: The paper defines the Velocity Ambiguity Profile (VAP) as the time-local Bayes-risk floor for velocity prediction. It decomposes the time-resolved loss into this intrinsic ambiguity and a reducible excess risk term, proving statistical benchmarks for Gaussian mixtures to validate the diagnostic.
technical_breakdown.architecture: No new model architecture is proposed; the method is a diagnostic framework applied to existing flow matching models, specifically tested on DINOv2 feature flows.
technical_breakdown.implementation_details: Key techniques include a dense transition sweep for validation, calibrated oracle-to-blind audits, and a guided time sampling strategy that prioritizes regions with high reducible error (low ambiguity) to optimize training efficiency.
technical_breakdown.code_complexity: The method adds a diagnostic layer to the training loop; computational overhead is associated with calculating the time-resolved loss decomposition and implementing the guided sampler, but it does not alter the underlying model inference complexity.

paper.title: SWE-DIVE: Multi-Turn Coding Agent Evaluation with Dynamic User Simulation
paper.summary: Coding agents are typically evaluated using one-shot, well-formulated prompts. Benchmarks such as SWE-bench use existing GitHub issues as input for a coding agent and evaluate whether the agent successfully solves the task. However, in real-world use cases, prompts are often not as well-formulated or structured as existing GitHub issues. Additionally, a coding agent session is not limited to a single prompt; it typically involves a multi-turn interaction in which the user iteratively adds new tasks and requirements that the agent must fulfill.   To benchmark these abilities, we developed SWE-DIVE, a dynamic, interactive validation and evaluation framework for benchmarking coding agents in a multi-turn environment. To achieve this, we introduce a user simulator that can simulate different behavioral patterns and communicate with the coding agent. We also introduce a conversation validator that evaluates the user simulator's outputs to determine whether they fulfill the initial requirements and guide the agent toward successfully solving the task. The entire framework is embedded in a Harbor environment, which orchestrates the coding agent, user simulator, and conversation validator, and executes the test environment to determine whether the agent successfully solves the task. Our results and source code are available in our GitHub repository (https://github.com/lorenzbrehme/swe-dive_usersim).
paper.comment: Accepted at the NeurIPS 2026 workshop "Grounded User Simulation for Model Evaluation and Training: Diversity, Fidelity, and Validity'' (non-archival)

analysis.problem_statement: Existing coding agent benchmarks rely on static, one-shot prompts that fail to capture the iterative, multi-turn nature of real-world software development interactions where requirements evolve dynamically.
analysis.bottleneck_addressed: Evaluation fidelity gap between static benchmark tasks and dynamic, multi-turn human-agent interaction patterns.
analysis.executive_summary: This paper addresses the limitation of current coding agent evaluations by introducing SWE-DIVE, a framework that simulates realistic multi-turn user interactions. It is significant because it moves beyond static issue-solving to test an agent's ability to handle iterative requirement changes and ambiguous initial prompts, which are critical for real-world deployment.

The validator specifically checks if the simulated user's outputs fulfill initial requirements and guide the agent toward a solution.

paper.title: Mitigating Model Collapse through Dreaming Learning
paper.summary: Training generative models on synthetic data causes loss of diversity and a decrease in performance, a phenomenon known as model collapse. We study this degeneration spectrally in a controlled Markov setting. The eigenvalue spectrum of the learned transition operator offers a direct view of the process, since the subdominant eigenvalues set how fast the chain mixes and therefore how much of the state space it continues to explore. We find that sampling at temperature $T_s < 1$ acts on the operator like repeated sharpening, pushing it toward a deterministic system: the subdominant eigenvalues approach the unit circle and the spectral gap narrows. When $T_s < 1$, even data accumulation does not appear to arrest this drift. We then analyze Dreaming Learning, a regulariser that, in parallel with regular training, adds a loss term on the model's own samples drawn at a raised temperature $T_d > 1$. Because high-temperature samples flatten the predicted distribution, training on them keeps the entries of the learned operator from becoming vanishingly small, which in turn keeps the eigenvalues bounded away from the unit circle. Measurements of the spectra over 5000 generations are consistent with this picture, and the mitigation effect persists in more complex settings such as LSTM language models and a 124M-parameter GPT-2.

analysis.executive_summary: This paper provides a spectral analysis of model collapse, identifying that low-temperature sampling causes the eigenvalues of the transition operator to approach the unit circle, effectively halting state space exploration. It proposes 'Dreaming Learning,' a regularization technique that uses high-temperature self-samples to maintain spectral gaps, thereby preserving diversity. The method demonstrates robust mitigation of collapse in both controlled Markov settings and large-scale language models like GPT-2.

paper.title: SCDM: Scalable Causal Discovery in Nonlinear Temporal Systems with Meta-Learning
paper.summary: Causal discovery from nonlinear multivariate time series is challenging in high-dimensional systems, where the number of candidate directed relations grows quadratically with the number of variables. Existing methods are often limited by target-wise model fitting, repeated conditional testing, or expensive graph-search procedures. We propose SCDM, a shared-parameter meta-learning framework for scalable temporal causal discovery. SCDM treats each target variable as a task while learning a shared temporal predictor and a shared causal-strength matrix across tasks. Each meta-episode updates only a subset of target-variable tasks, allowing the model to accumulate structural evidence across the full system without exhaustive target-wise optimization. After training, a post-training graph readout converts the learned predictor into continuous directed causal scores for threshold-independent evaluation. We also provide a finite-error recovery principle showing that, under fully observed delayed-system assumptions and a positive risk-gap condition, thresholding SCDM scores recovers the graph when statistical, meta-optimization, and readout errors are below the population margin. Experiments on controlled synthetic, neuroimaging-inspired, high-dimensional, and real-world temporal benchmarks demonstrate competitive causal recovery and improved scalability in large temporal systems.

analysis.executive_summary: SCDM introduces a meta-learning framework that decouples causal discovery from exhaustive target-wise optimization by sharing parameters across tasks. This approach enables scalable structural learning in large temporal systems, addressing a critical gap in applying causal AI to complex, high-dimensional real-world data like neuroimaging.

paper.title: Your Benchmark Is an Empirical Measure Over Difficulty
paper.summary: A benchmark is not merely a collection of test questions; it naturally induces an empirical measure over difficulty. In this work, we develop this measure-based view of benchmark evaluation. This perspective allows us to identify and formalize two central failure modes: measure mismatch, where the benchmark difficulty distribution differs from the intended difficulty distribution, and coverage gaps, where uncovered regions along the difficulty axis prevent benchmarks from detecting meaningful localized training progress. We propose two diagnostic metrics that capture these two failure modes and provide rigorous theoretical guarantees. Empirically, we analyze 25 popular benchmarks spanning 7 domains using carefully estimated item difficulties. Our results show that many benchmarks implicitly overweight certain difficulty regions, so their leaderboard conclusions should be interpreted with caution; others leave substantial portions of the difficulty axis uncovered, limiting their ability to monitor the model improvement process. Finally, we turn diagnosis into action by introducing BenchFill, a simple difficulty-targeted item rewriting algorithm that effectively reduces local coverage gaps.

This perspective reveals that current leaderboard rankings may not reflect true model capabilities across the full spectrum of task difficulty, necessitating a shift from simple accuracy metrics to distribution-aware evaluation.

paper.title: Privacy in Context Is Being Overlooked in the Age of General-Purpose LLMs
paper.summary: As large language models (LLMs) continue to grow in scope and capability, privacy concerns are on the rise. Since users increasingly interact with a single general-purpose system across many distinct contexts, there is a natural tendency to pursue a one-size-fits-all solution to privacy. Unfortunately, this overlooks a crucial insight from decades of privacy research: privacy is inherently contextual. In this paper, we argue that existing work in prompt privacy is drifting towards attempts to design a unified framework, which is highly misleading and can foster a false sense of security. Furthermore, we argue that even future work in this direction needs to wrestle with fundamental tensions across various desirable properties of prompt privacy. Thus, such continued attempts towards a unified framework need to be reconsidered. We recommend three critical paths forward: application-specific deployment of LLMs, context-specific evaluation of privacy frameworks, and better privacy literacy.

paper.title: Real PMIDs, Wrong Papers: Harness Design for Biomedical Claim-Verification Agents
paper.summary: Literature-searching language agents are becoming a standard component of scientific assistants for the life sciences, yet there is little controlled evidence on which parts of their harness matter. We run a controlled ablation on biomedical claim verification (SciFact) with the live PubMed API as the only tool. Holding the backbone and output format fixed, we compare four harnesses: closed-book answering, single-shot retrieval using the claim as the query, a ReAct-style agent that writes its own PubMed queries, and an oracle given the gold abstracts, each with two efficient frontier backbones. Naive single-shot retrieval finds the gold paper for only 6% of claims and turns overconfident errors into abstentions without improving accuracy. Letting the model formulate its own queries triples gold recall and yields the best verdicts (62% accuracy vs. 49-59% for the other realistic harnesses), although these differences are not significant at our sample size and agents use fewer than half of their search budget. With gold abstracts, the same models reach 79-86% accuracy, a significant 17-24 point gap showing that retrieval, not reasoning, is the main bottleneck. Finally, a citation audit shows that closed-book models cite PubMed IDs that almost always exist (327/335) but are almost never relevant: a cross-family LLM judge rates only 3 of 327 existing citations as relevant to the claim, versus 67% for citations produced by the search agent. Existence checks are therefore insufficient safeguards for scientific agents. We release code, prompts, and all cached tool calls at https://github.com/saqlain2204/real-pmids-wrong-papers.

It demonstrates that allowing agents to autonomously formulate queries significantly improves performance, but the largest accuracy gap remains between retrieval-augmented agents and those with oracle access to gold abstracts, proving that retrieval is the dominant bottleneck over reasoning.

paper.title: UniRAP: Towards Unified Part-level Physical Affordance Reasoning and Actionable Perception
paper.summary: Vision-language perception has achieved impressive progress in aligning natural language with visual observations, yet grounding high-level semantics into part-level physical interaction remains challenging. To address this gap, we propose UniRAP, a unified model for inferring part-level physical affordances and mapping language instructions to actionable geometric representations. UniRAP formulates this problem as a conditional multimodal generation task, integrating visual inputs, textual instructions, and optional prompts into a shared spatiotemporal representation space through a unified interface token mechanism. To predict executable contact geometry, we introduce a Unified Affordance Decoder (UAD), which jointly performs object detection, part-level affordance segmentation, and 4-DoF interaction pose estimation by leveraging intermediate segmentation features. In addition, we propose a curriculum-based transfer training strategy that progressively adapts the model from general visual parsing to interaction-aware perception, improving data efficiency under limited textual annotations. Experiments show that UniRAP achieves state-of-the-art performance on referring expression segmentation, affordance grounding, and interaction pose estimation, while maintaining strong spatiotemporal consistency in dynamic video scenarios. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of UniRAP as a unified perception framework for language-guided physical manipulation.

paper.title: FogTTA: Online Test-Time Adaptation for Robust Transformer-based Object Detection in Foggy Weather
paper.summary: Object detection models for autonomous driving commonly experience substantial performance drops when deployed under adverse weather due to the domain shift between training data and real-world operating conditions. This degradation is especially evident when models trained on clear-weather images encounter foggy environments with reduced visibility and contrast. To address this challenge, we introduce FogTTA, an online test-time adaptation framework designed to improve the robustness of Transformer-based object detectors in fog. Using RF-DETR as the underlying object detector, FogTTA enables real-time adaptation to the streaming target domain without requiring source data or retraining. The framework follows a teacher-student design, where the deployed model serves as the teacher and generates pseudo labels from weakly augmented target inputs. These predictions are subsequently refined through non-maximum suppression and confidence filtering. The student model then learns from strongly augmented target sample using the Varifocal loss to mitigate pseudo-label noise. The teacher is updated via exponential moving averaging to ensure stable and continuous adaptation. Experiments show that FogTTA outperforms prior baselines, delivering improved detection accuracy and stability while maintaining real-time performance.

paper.title: The Reflexivity Threshold: A Phase Transition for Multi-Agent Performative Prediction
paper.summary: Many learning systems are performative: once deployed, their predictions change the data distribution on which future models are trained. In multi-agent settings, this feedback is routed through a network of interacting learners, so stability depends not only on the strength of performativity but also on who affects whom. We study repeated retraining in multi-agent performative prediction and identify a spectral threshold that separates stable learning from worst-case learning obstruction. Prior work often collapses cross-agent feedback into a scalar contraction constant, missing this network structure. We instead introduce the reflexivity matrix $Γ$, which records how strongly one agent's deployment can move another agent's best response, defined from per-agent gradient sensitivities and curvature parameters. The threshold occurs when the spectral radius of this matrix crosses one. Below the threshold, repeated retraining converges geometrically to a unique performatively stable equilibrium, with cumulative excess loss bounded uniformly in the time horizon. Above the threshold, we construct noisy supercritical instances in which every local-information learner incurs expected cumulative excess loss growing linearly for horizons up to order $1/(ρ(Γ)-1)$. Together, these results characterize the threshold behavior through upper and lower bounds and recover the single-agent scalar threshold from prior work as a special case.

analysis.executive_summary: This paper identifies a spectral threshold for the reflexivity matrix that determines whether multi-agent performative learning converges or diverges. It demonstrates that network structure, rather than just scalar contraction constants, dictates stability, providing a rigorous boundary between stable and obstructed learning regimes.

paper.title: Shortcut-Resistant CAM Distillation for Long-Tailed Recognition
paper.summary: Real-world datasets often follow a long-tailed distribution, making generalization to tail classes difficult. We revisit this problem through the lens of shortcut learning, where models prefer the easiest predictive cues (e.g., background or textures) over object-centric semantics, especially under scarce and biased supervision. We find that this tendency is amplified for tail classes: limited examples often share similar contexts, making non-semantic signals highly correlated and thus tempting shortcuts, whereas head classes with diverse appearances and environments encourage more stable object-focused representations. Motivated by this observation, we propose Shortcut-Resistant CAM Distillation (SRCD), a plug-and-play framework that transfers object-focused explanations from head to tail classes. SRCD operates in the Class Activation Map (CAM) space, where a CAM provides a class-specific spatial evidence map for a prediction. SRCD aggregates CAMs from a small set of head-class candidates into a shortcut-resistant teacher using an energy-model weighting based on coherence and concentration, and distills it to the tail-class CAM. We provide a theoretical analysis that quantifies shortcut reliance as shortcut-region evidence mass in CAM space and shows that SRCD suppresses tail shortcuts. Extensive experiments on long-tailed benchmarks consistently improve strong baselines. The code is available at https://github.com/Haifeng3/SRCD.

paper.title: Rethinking Agentic Model Orchestration for Time Series Forecasting
paper.summary: Time series foundation models (TSFMs) perform unevenly across forecasting tasks. Recent work uses agentic model orchestration (AMO) to select or combine TSFMs, often outperforming individual forecasters. Yet these gains may reflect stronger or more complementary candidates rather than better orchestration. To disentangle these effects, we introduce FairAMO, a controlled evaluation protocol with frozen candidate forecasts. Experiments on GIFT-Eval show that AMO improves accuracy, but its gains are bounded by the candidate TSFMs. The best orchestrators reduce MASE by less than 6% relative to the best single TSFM across all tasks. These gains depend on complementarity (different candidates excel on different tasks) rather than the number of candidates. Adding members yields diminishing returns, and a redundant member can erase these gains. The value of historical evidence also saturates quickly. A few recent windows capture all gains, and further history adds none. These findings separate system-level forecasting gains from the contribution of orchestration itself.

paper.title: OmniSimulator: Aligning Small Language Models for Authentic Heterogeneous Behavior Modeling
paper.summary: Large language models (LLMs) have shown great potential as general-purpose user simulators for interactive systems. Prior studies have demonstrated that training on high-quality data can substantially improve model reasoning and downstream task performance. However, the upper bound of user simulation is still constrained by the model's reasoning paradigm: native chain-of-thought often degenerates into shallow pattern matching and fails to adequately model the behavioral factors underlying real user decisions. In this paper, we propose OmniSimulator, a novel training framework designed to improve the predictive ability of small LLMs for realistic user simulation on short-video platform environments. Specifically, OmniSimulator organizes behavior-oriented reasoning through a structured schema with five dimensions, carefully selects data from real user-behavior scenarios, and introduces a teacher model to generate high-quality reasoning traces under the proposed schema, helping small models learn behavior-relevant reasoning patterns rather than relying on superficial behavioral correlations. Based on this process, we construct 9,881 high-quality training instances from three months of historical interaction trajectories of 200 real users, averaging about 50 distilled examples per user. Experimental results show that OmniSimulator improves the average score of Qwen3-8B by 34.33%, achieves performance competitive with Claude-Sonnet-4.5, and supports smaller-scale, self-hosted deployment. These results suggest that learning structured behavior-oriented reasoning patterns is a promising direction towards scalable and high-fidelity LLM-based user simulation.

analysis.executive_summary: This paper addresses the limitation of small LLMs in user simulation by introducing a structured, behavior-oriented reasoning framework that moves beyond pattern matching. paper.title: PreCoMem: Predictive Cognitive Memory for Self-Evolving Long-Term Dialogue Agents
paper.summary: Long-horizon dialogue agents need to keep user memories stable enough for personalization while adapting when the user genuinely changes. Existing memory systems often append every observation or overwrite old entries by heuristic rules, which makes transient noise hard to distinguish from real belief drift. We introduce PreCoMem, a memory consolidation framework inspired by predictive coding that represents memory as confidence-weighted beliefs about the user's state. Its core signal, Effective Surprisal, combines semantic deviation and contradiction evidence, then downweights this signal when retrieval is diffuse and unreliable. According to effective surprisal, a two-threshold gate maps each turn to one of three deterministic updates: MAINTAIN reinforces supported beliefs, PROFILE stores ambiguous cues as low-confidence hypotheses, and CORRECT softly decays reliably contradicted facts. The PROFILE stage acts as an explicit waiting room, preventing premature commitment to noisy evidence. Experiments on LoCoMo, LongMemEval-S, and PersonaMem-v2 show consistent state-of-the-art accuracy; our new DiMoBench confirms that PreCoMem adapts to non-stationary belief drift without over-reacting to noise. The code is available at https://github.com/ZhongWishing/PreCoMem.

paper.title: BIRD-RL: Scaling Agentic Reinforcement Learning over Stateful Data-Centric Environments
paper.summary: While agentic reinforcement learning (RL) has emerged as a promising paradigm for training small language models (SLMs), existing frameworks are predominantly tool-centric and struggle with data-centric environments. Specifically, applying tool-centric frameworks to stateful tasks like SQL debugging introduces severe spatial inefficiencies since proper environment isolation typically requires a separate database container per rollout. Naively reusing databases without tracking evolving states across multi-turn interactions causes trajectory contamination and cross-trajectory interference, which severely destabilizes policy updates. To overcome these bottlenecks, we introduce BIRD-RL, a novel four-stage agentic RL curriculum that alternately enhances foundational agent reasoning and trajectory-adaptive on-policy exploration to circumvent the instability inherently associated with direct end-to-end learning. Crucially, to support this curriculum, BIRD-RL is driven by a Trajectory-scoped Persistent Execution Infrastructure, which enables safe database replica reuse while preserving trajectory isolation. This design improves spatial RL efficiency by 12.8x, successfully enabling scalable agentic RL for complex data-centric tasks without needs of Kubernettes. Empirical evaluations on the BIRD-CRITIC-SQLite benchmark demonstrate that our 7B and 14B models achieve Success Rates of 44.40% and 48.00%, respectively, showing competitive performance against strong proprietary model-based agents such as Claude-Opus-4.6 Agent (48.20%). Furthermore, BIRD-RL successfully trains unified SLMs capable of both advanced SQL debugging and generation, highlighting its broader potential for multi-objective optimization across heterogeneous, real-world data-centric tasks.

paper.title: Benchmarking and Error Analysis of Deep Search and Deep Research LLM Agents
paper.summary: As Large Language Models (LLMs) evolve into autonomous Deep Search and Deep Research Agents capable of executing long-horizon, multi-step tasks, evaluating their reliability becomes increasingly critical. However, existing evaluation paradigms predominantly focus on final task outcomes, leaving a significant gap in understanding the intermediate execution traces, where agents are highly susceptible to various errors. To address this critical gap, we introduce a comprehensive methodology and analytical framework designed specifically to diagnose errors in intermediate workflows. Building upon this framework, we establish a structured taxonomy that categorizes these vulnerabilities into two primary dimensions: System-Level Errors and Task-Level Errors. Through a systematic examination of step-by-step execution traces and agent-environment interactions, we reveal how these underlying errors affect overall performance. Finally, through empirical experiments and systematic analysis of the identified error types, we provide actionable design guidelines, aiming to enhance the robustness, reasoning capabilities, and reliability of Deep Search and Deep Research agents.

paper.title: A Stratified Multi-Rater Evaluation of LLM-Based Virtual Standardized Patients with a Deployed Data-Generation Platform
paper.summary: The Objective Structured Clinical Examination (OSCE) is widely used to assess clinical communication skills in medical education, requiring trainees to take histories and reason clinically with standardized patients (SPs). Large language model (LLM)-based virtual standardized patients (VSPs), typically built by persona-injected prompting, offer a practical alternative. However, existing evaluations rely on a single backbone LLM, small human rater panels, or LLM-as-a-judge scoring without an utterance-aligned human-expert reference, and so cannot identify the specific shortcomings of individual models. We evaluated four LLMs (GPT-4o, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, Llama-3.1 70B, and HyperCLOVA X), spanning commercial, open-source and Korean-developed models, against a human-expert reference across three Korean OSCE cases (hematuria, fever in pregnancy, and chronic cough). In a double-blind, fully crossed design, 17 senior medical-student raters scored every model utterance on three sentence-level and six encounter-level Likert metrics, yielding 7,480 data points. We analyzed the scores using a stratified linear mixed-effects model based on an 11-category history-taking and 3-level linguistic-form taxonomy. At the encounter level, three of the four LLMs fell 0.08 to 0.47 Likert points below the human-expert reference on Comprehensibility, Consistency and Hallucination-freeness. The difference was not statistically significant for Hallucination-freeness in Claude 3.5 Sonnet and GPT-4o, Consistency in GPT-4o, and Engagement in HyperCLOVA X. Llama-3.1 70B fell significantly below the reference on all six metrics. We also introduce a web-based OSCE platform that supports virtual practice across diverse clinical cases and continuously collects student-VSP dialogues under research and privacy consent.

paper.title: A Unified Evaluation Framework of Physical Adversarial Robustness in the Edge VLM Era
paper.summary: Recent advancements in Vision-Language Models (VLMs) enable end-to-end visual grounding via language prompts and generative decoding, demonstrating largely improved zero-shot and open-vocabulary detection capabilities. As a result, VLMs are rapidly being deployed at the edge in safety-critical real-world systems. However, the physical adversarial robustness of edge VLMs has not been systematically studied, and the fundamental differences in output with modern object detectors create methodological challenges for fair evaluation. To compare the two families directly, we evaluate every selected representative model on one outcome: whether an adversarial patch worn on a person evades detection of the model. We report this by introducing a unified metric, conditional attack success rate (cASR), counted only on images the model still localizes under a matched gray occluder, and partition every failure into omission (no box), substitution (a box on the patch), and displacement (a box on neither). We benchmark the physical adversarial vulnerability of compact grounding VLMs against a range of object detectors, and find that the VLMs can be as vulnerable as the detectors. We disclose that failure mode is largely associated with the output format of a model rather than its architecture family. Of the three, only omission is visible to a downstream system; displacement and substitution return confident, well-formed boxes, making them potentially more dangerous failures. Further, we find that, under distribution shift, VLMs that primarily failed by omission instead shift to failing more by displacement/substitution. Thus, a grounding VLM can inherit the detector's vulnerability while showing the possibility to adopt more dangerous failure modes. Our code and data are available at https://github.com/ericliang1/physical-adversarial-robustness.

It introduces a unified metric (cASR) that exposes how VLMs can exhibit more dangerous failure modes (substitution/displacement) than detectors, particularly under distribution shift, which traditional evaluation metrics might miss.

paper.title: SU(2)-Equivariant Spinor Message Passing for Molecular Magnetism
paper.summary: Predicting molecular magnetism often requires electronic-structure calculations with spin-orbit coupling (SOC), which are costly to repeat across many molecules. The underlying electronic states can transform as spinors, yet equivariant surrogates typically use only integer-rank features. Inspired by the spinor nature of these electronic states, we develop eSpinor, an SU(2)-equivariant graph neural network that propagates spinor features. We initialize spinor features from eigenvectors of an approximate SOC Hamiltonian and use gauge-covariant message passing with a gauge-invariant readout to make predictions independent of the arbitrary eigenbasis choice. On cobalt single-molecule magnet candidates, eSpinor improves zero-field-splitting predictions relative to NequIP, including for unseen ligands. For a dysprosium magnetic resonance imaging probe, eSpinor improves real electron-spin correlations over a Hamiltonian-informed baseline despite similar static crystal-field errors and fewer parameters, while accurately predicting low-field nuclear relaxation in water and after transfer to methanol without retraining. Overall, these results demonstrate that SU(2)-equivariant spinor message passing is a useful inductive bias for molecular magnetism. We also find that similar static tensor errors can yield different dynamical errors, motivating model selection based on accuracy for the intended physical observables.

By using gauge-covariant message passing, it achieves accurate predictions of dynamic magnetic properties with fewer parameters than baseline models, demonstrating that equivariant surrogates can effectively replace costly SOC calculations.

paper.title: PhyMo: Learning Physical Dynamics with Accurate and Continuous Motion from Multi-View Videos
paper.summary: Recovering dynamic 3D scene geometry, appearance, and the physical motion states that govern scene evolution from multi-view videos is important yet challenging. A key difficulty is that appearance can be deceptive. Under rendering supervision alone, a model may fit the observed images by changing color or opacity to compensate for inaccurate deformation, rather than recovering the true evolving geometry and motion. This issue is especially severe in scenes with fast or locally complex motion, where inaccurate trajectories can still produce plausible images over the observed frames, but lead to unreliable reconstruction and discontinuous future prediction. In this paper, we propose PhyMo, a framework for learning evolving dynamics from multi-view videos. We introduce a Motion-Aware Trajectory Representation that drives the model to recover accurate motion from deformation, rather than relying on appearance shortcuts to explain observed motion. On top of this, we propose a Continuous Motion Evolution module with bidirectional kinematic continuity constraint to promote temporally consistent evolution of displacement, velocity, and acceleration. Together, these designs yield geometrically faithful interpolation and continuous motion extrapolation. Experiments on four dynamic scene benchmarks demonstrate state-of-the-art performance.

analysis.executive_summary: This paper addresses a critical limitation in dynamic 3D reconstruction where rendering supervision alone leads to physically inaccurate motion due to appearance compensation. By enforcing motion-aware trajectory representations and kinematic continuity, PhyMo ensures that the recovered dynamics are geometrically faithful and temporally consistent. This is significant for advancing autonomous systems and robotics that rely on reliable physical state estimation from visual data.

paper.title: Distilling Multi-Teacher Scoring Principles for Unsupervised Time Series Anomaly Detection
paper.summary: Time series anomalies take diverse forms, and individual detectors encode different anomaly scoring principles that rarely cover all anomaly types. Recent unsupervised time-series anomaly detectors provide complementary scoring signals, yet deploying them as an ensemble preserves the inference and maintenance cost of every individual detector. We study whether heterogeneous teacher detectors can be distilled into a single lightweight detector in the unsupervised setting, where no anomaly labels are available to define a shared target. AnoMix addresses this by extracting weak pairwise supervision from the training-set anomaly scores of frozen teachers. It normalizes each teacher score sequence independently and trains the student with CoRank, a multi-teacher ranking-distillation objective that converts teacher score gaps into pairwise supervision through teacher consensus. Across seven benchmark datasets, AnoMix successfully integrates complementary teacher scoring principles into a single deployable model, improving over individual detectors and static score ensembles while using a compact student with under 80k parameters on the benchmark settings. A zero-shot variant further shows that the distilled ranking signal transfers to unseen datasets and can outperform large pretrained time-series foundation models for anomaly detection.

paper.title: Fast Template Matching for Quantum Circuits Using Hypergraph
paper.summary: Quantum circuit optimization is a key step toward the efficient execution of quantum algorithms. Template matching has emerged as one of the dominant approaches for simplifying quantum circuits, yet it confronts the intrinsic challenge of accommodating gate commutativity. The state-of-the-art template-matching algorithm relies on a directed acyclic graph (DAG) representation. While this DAG-based technique handles gate commutativity satisfactorily, it fails to preserve the local connectivity inherent to quantum circuits, thereby leading to relatively high matching complexity.   In this paper, we introduce a hypergraph representation (HG), a commutativity-aware representation that collapses commuting gates into a single super-node while retaining all local connectivity. This enables matches to be extended locally without revisiting the rest of the circuit, with incremental updates limited to the immediate neighborhood. Experimental results demonstrate that our HG matcher achieves 11--606x speed-up over the DAG-based implementation in Qiskit (Iten et al., 2022) on both random and arithmetic benchmarks, while maintaining the same optimization quality. The acceleration increases with circuit size, confirming that preserving locality and connectivity is the key to scalable quantum circuit optimisation.

paper.title: Building Auditable AI Text Detectors with Sparse Autoencoders
paper.summary: AI-generated text detectors are increasingly deployed in consequential settings---peer review, education, admissions, journalism, and content moderation---where their outputs directly affect individuals. Yet the strongest detectors are fine-tuned neural classifiers whose decisions are opaque, while transparent alternatives (stylometric and linguistic-feature classifiers) underperform them by wide margins. We present a pipeline that converts a fine-tuned neural detector into a classifier that operates on human-readable concepts. We accomplish this by training sparse autoencoders (SAEs) directly on a detector's residual stream, assigning auto-interpretation labels to each SAE feature, and retaining only features whose generated descriptions pass a global fidelity threshold. We then train a lightweight classifier on just the interpretable features. We find that our SAEs recover latent concepts that correspond to highly specific and predictive linguistic "tells" of AI-generated text. Classifiers built on these extracted features are not only highly interpretable but exhibit stronger performance on out-of-distribution texts than either neural or stylometric alternatives.

paper.title: Graph Topology Meets Energy-Driven Pathfinding: Preserving Contextual Consistency in Retrieval-Augmented Generation
paper.summary: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) frequently integrates knowledge graphs (KGs) for complex multi-hop question answering. However, their performance is increasingly bottlenecked by the knowledge structuring and reasoning processes. (i) Severe semantic loss: Distilling continuous texts into discrete symbols strips away contextual nuances and narrative coherence. (ii) Pronounced modality mismatch: Fragmented graph structures clash with the continuous texts LLMs are pre-trained on, while rewriting them into natural language introduces generative noise and omits information. To address these limitations, we propose ThreadRAG, a semantic-topology-based RAG framework for context-preserving knowledge structuring and modality-native evidence reasoning. ThreadRAG introduces a Semantic Topology Mapper (STM), which organizes retrieved documents into context-intact Semantic Nodes and constructs a Semantic Topology Graph (STG) through narrative, semantic, and lexical edges. It further incorporates Energy-Driven Pathfinding (EDP), which identifies query-relevant subgraphs via energy diffusion and deterministically linearizes them into coherent textual evidence paths. Experiments on three multi-hop QA benchmarks demonstrate that ThreadRAG consistently outperforms strong baselines. Notably, it achieves a 14.4% EM improvement over text-centric methods on HotpotQA and surpasses the best baseline by 5.8% EM on 2WikiMultihop, while reducing token cost to 23.3% of the strongest baseline.

analysis.bottleneck_addressed: Contextual consistency and modality alignment in multi-hop reasoning pipelines.
analysis.executive_summary: This paper addresses the critical gap in RAG systems where converting text to knowledge graphs strips away narrative coherence, leading to degraded performance in complex question answering. By preserving contextual integrity through a semantic topology approach, it enables more accurate and token-efficient reasoning without the generative noise associated with graph-to-text rewriting.

technical_breakdown.implementation_details: Uses narrative, semantic, and lexical edges for graph construction; employs energy diffusion for subgraph identification; deterministic linearization for evidence path generation.
technical_breakdown.code_complexity: Reduces token cost to 23.3% of the strongest baseline, implying significant computational efficiency in inference.

paper.title: WRDO: Weighted Refusal Direction Optimization in Aligned Language Models
paper.summary: Aligned large language models are trained to comply with benign requests while refusing harmful ones. However, recent work shows that this refusal behavior is fragile and can often be disrupted by simple activation- or weight-space interventions. In particular, refusal has been shown to be largely mediated by a single residual-stream direction, typically computed as a difference-of-means vector between harmful and harmless prompts. However, this standard construction aggregates heterogeneous harmful prompts into one uniform average, potentially conflating distinct refusal-related phenomena. In this work, we study whether refusal interventions can be strengthened by learning how to combine prompt-specific refusal directions. We propose Weighted Refusal Direction Optimization (WRDO), a procedure that constructs a composite refusal direction from a bank of per-prompt directions using learned aggregation weights. This approach allows different harmful prompts to contribute unequally to the final intervention direction. We evaluate WRDO against prior single-direction methods on three open-weight language models using three guard judges and HarmBench as an external evaluator. We further measure the effect of the intervention on general model capability through standard utility benchmarks. Finally, we investigate a defense-oriented setting in which the same optimization machinery is used in reverse to restore refusal behavior in an abliterated model checkpoint. Our results show that weighted aggregation provides a more effective and flexible mechanism for manipulating refusal representations.

analysis.bottleneck_addressed: Robustness of safety alignment and the fragility of refusal mechanisms against weight-space interventions.
analysis.executive_summary: This work addresses the vulnerability of current LLM safety mechanisms by demonstrating that refusal is mediated by a single residual-stream direction that can be easily disrupted. By proposing Weighted Refusal Direction Optimization (WRDO), the paper offers a more flexible and effective method for manipulating refusal representations, enhancing both the robustness of safety interventions and the ability to restore refusal in abliterated models.

paper.title: VIRA-Bench: Diagnosing Pedagogical Contingency Understanding in Online Tutoring Videos
paper.summary: Understanding a one-to-one tutoring video requires more than recognizing its events. A model must connect a visible teacher intervention to the learner response it elicits and to the follow-up adjusted to that response. Existing video and educational-dialogue benchmarks typically emphasize event recognition, temporal reasoning, social-state inference, or transcript-based interaction, but rarely diagnose this action-response-adjustment relation. We introduce VIRA-Bench, a focused diagnostic benchmark for short-horizon pedagogical contingency in one-to-one online tutoring. VIRA-Bench contains 1,005 tutoring clips and 1,322 multiple-choice questions with researcher evidence audit and expert verification, organized into Observable Evidence Grounding (OEG), Interaction Contingency Reasoning (ICR), and Support-Response Modeling (SRM). Across 11 models, the best reaches 61.3%, well below the 91.0% human reference on a stratified subset, and ICR generally has the lowest layer accuracy among leading models. Under controlled input manipulations, removing video most strongly degrades OEG, whereas disrupting temporal order most strongly degrades ICR. Free-response, Stem+Options, and synchronized-shuffle controls show that response format, static question cues, and video-ASR mismatch do not explain these layer-specific patterns. The results identify distinct behavioral evidence dependencies without claiming an internal architectural mechanism. VIRA-Bench provides a focused evaluation resource for multimodal dialogue grounding, pedagogical discourse, and temporal reasoning in online tutoring.

analysis.executive_summary: This paper introduces VIRA-Bench, a diagnostic benchmark designed to test if AI models can link visible teacher actions to specific learner responses and follow-up adjustments. It reveals a significant performance gap between the best AI models (61.3%) and human experts (91.0%), highlighting that current models struggle with interaction contingency reasoning (ICR) and rely heavily on video evidence for grounding observable facts.

paper.title: Policy Central: Detecting Conflicts, Redundancy, and Similarity in Deployed Police Policy
paper.summary: Policy Central is a deployed system that helps police departments find relationships between sections of their written policy: whether two sections conflict, are redundant, are merely similar, or are different. We describe the system and compare two architectures. Retrieve-Judge, a retrieve-then-classify pipeline, runs as a cheap library-wide health signal; Screen-Confirm, a screen-then-confirm cascade, is a selective audit of the documents a reviewer chooses, checking them exhaustively against one another. On a 302-pair benchmark drawn from one department's ~84 real policy documents, given each pair Screen-Confirm reaches 0.795 aggregate recall and 0.885 on Conflict, so current models judge well. Finding the pair is the hard part: Retrieve-Judge's composed recall falls to 0.457, and Screen-Confirm recovers 0.472 (0.615 on Conflict). Today these pairs are found by reading the whole library, nearly 20,000 sections, checked against one another and re-checked after every revision. A scan that returns half of them in minutes, at low cost, and can be re-run on demand changes the economics of policy review even before recall improves.
paper.comment: 16 pages, 2 figures. Committed to EACL 2027

analysis.problem_statement: The paper addresses the computational and economic infeasibility of manually auditing large-scale police policy libraries for conflicts, redundancy, and similarity due to the quadratic complexity of checking all section pairs.
analysis.bottleneck_addressed: Scalability of exhaustive pairwise comparison in large document corpora and the high cost of manual legal/policy review.
analysis.executive_summary: This work introduces 'Policy Central,' a deployed system that automates the detection of logical relationships (conflict, redundancy, similarity) within police policy documents. It demonstrates that while current LLMs are effective at judging specific pairs, the primary bottleneck is retrieval; however, even a system that recovers only ~50% of relevant pairs in minutes significantly improves the economics of policy maintenance compared to manual full-library reviews.

technical_breakdown.implementation_details: The system was tested on a 302-pair benchmark derived from ~84 real policy documents from a single department. technical_breakdown.code_complexity: The system reduces the operational complexity from checking ~20,000 sections against one another (quadratic growth) to a scalable scan that runs in minutes at low cost, enabling on-demand re-evaluation after revisions.

paper.title: OSynth: A Longitudinal, Context-Sensitive Evaluation of Meeting Understanding
paper.summary: Meeting notetakers are increasingly deployed in settings where longitudinal context is available including calendar metadata, prior meetings, emails, slides, and speaker enrollments; however, meeting corpora remain limited in terms of size, domain coverage, and available context. We present OSynth, a large-scale synthetic dataset of simulated organizations comprising 570 hours of meeting audio together with associated artifacts and a latent ground-truth state. In a pairwise comparison, human raters distinguish OSynth meetings from real meeting transcripts with only 56% accuracy based on excerpts of 150-300 words. Across state-of-the-art LLMs, additional context yields significant gains on several entity-sensitive dimensions, demonstrating limitations of contemporary approaches and the potential usefulness of OSynth in developing better-contextualized meeting-understanding systems.

By providing a large-scale synthetic dataset with latent ground-truth states, it enables the rigorous evaluation of how additional context (emails, slides, history) impacts model performance, revealing that current LLMs still struggle with entity-sensitive dimensions despite contextual inputs.

paper.title: LTEM: LLM-Friendly Table-Enhanced Markdown for Table Understanding and Generation
paper.summary: Tables in real-world documents, including scientific papers, financial reports, and statistical summaries, frequently use merged cells, multi-level headers, and sectioned layouts. Yet the lightweight formats LLMs handle best (Markdown, CSV) cannot express these structures, while expressive formats (HTML, LaTeX) impose excessive token cost and parsing complexity. To enable systematic analysis of this trade-off, we introduce a taxonomy decomposing table structure into six atomic features (F1-F6) and corresponding complexity levels (L1-L6), and construct STB (Synthetic Table Benchmark), a controlled benchmark with 1,089 tables systematically distributed across complexity levels. Using this framework, we propose LTEM (LLM-friendly Table-Enhanced Markdown), a formally specified, minimal extension of Markdown that explicitly encodes spans and hierarchical headers. Experiments across five state-of-the-art LLMs show that LTEM achieves accuracy comparable to HTML, offers a favorable accuracy-token trade-off relative to HTML and LaTeX, and produces substantially fewer invalid responses than LaTeX; for table generation, LTEM is comparable to MultiMarkdown though HTML is best. We release our taxonomy, benchmark, and format specification to support future research on LLM-table interaction.

analysis.executive_summary: This paper addresses the critical gap in LLM-table interaction by introducing LTEM, a minimal Markdown extension that encodes complex table structures with lower token overhead than HTML or LaTeX. It provides a systematic framework (taxonomy and benchmark) to evaluate this trade-off, enabling more efficient and accurate table understanding and generation in resource-constrained LLM environments.

paper.title: Multi-level Encoder with Global Topic for Task-oriented Dialogue Summarization
paper.summary: Task-oriented dialogue summarization aims to automatically extract key information to generate domain summaries to improve service efficiency and quality. Task-oriented dialogue is inherently logical and surrounds specific topic. How to effectively capture the dialogue topic and the most salient information becomes one of the major challenges of this task. In this paper, we propose a task-oriented dialogue summarization model utilizing a multi-level encoder with global topic (MLEGT). This model discovers temporal and spatial dependencies through a multi-level encoder, while simultaneously obtaining a simple yet effective global topic in the process of graph construction. It not only captures the crucial details but also breaks the long-range limit and discover the intrinsic structure across the dialogue. Then, a global topic guided pointer mechanism is added into the summrizer to capture ignored but important information, which is helpful to improve the accuracy of the summary. A comprehensive study of two public datasets, including a real-world large-scale Chinese police interrogation dataset and a medical reporting service dataset proves the superiority of our method on several strong baselines.

By addressing the limitation of local attention mechanisms in capturing intrinsic dialogue structures, the method enhances summary accuracy for high-stakes applications like police interrogation and medical reporting.

paper.title: VeriEvolve: Evaluator-First Evolution for Tool-Using Agents
paper.summary: A central obstacle to self-improving agents is the absence of a reliable fitness signal for realistic stateful tasks. We introduce \textsc{VeriEvolve}, an evaluator-first evolution framework that constructs this missing evaluation layer before optimizing the agent. From task instruction, VeriEvolve synthesizes instruction-grounded challenge states and an executable evaluator that checks them. During each round of workflow evolution, the evaluator is frozen and serves as the fitness signal. Between rounds, VeriEvolve revises the evaluator by converting the end states of strong and weak runs into a pair of counterfactual test cases.   Across all 30 MCPMark Filesystem tasks, VeriEvolve constructs 30 evaluators with 141 challenge states, achieving 141/141 agreement on the generated suites and 113/122 agreement on held-out states produced by executor agents. Evaluator-guided evolution increases externally verified success from 6/30 to 18/30 for GLM-5.2 and from 27/30 to 30/30 for Claude; refinement removes all three false positives that the weak executor exposes. Cross-environment studies on PostgreSQL, Playwright, Notion, and GitHub further expose complementary limits from observability, state representation, and search/execution capacity. These results show that executable evaluators can be synthesized and used to guide search when task success is observable and an external verifier is available for calibration.

By freezing the evaluator during optimization and refining it between rounds using counterfactual test cases, the method significantly improves the success rate of tool-using agents on complex filesystem tasks.
